_schema.communication.preferredFormat: pictures | voice | text | story — this alone decides how answers arrive

report.name: Alberto Ruiz
report.author: Dr Lina Moreau
report.summary: Alberto is an autistic adult working full time in a warehouse team. He follows procedures accurately and holds detail well once it is learned. Difficulty is almost always with how instructions arrive, not with the task itself. Verbal instructions given at speed, in noisy areas, or bundled together are the main source of breakdown. When the same instruction is given visually and in small pieces, retention is excellent.

notes: Three SPOKEN steps at a time is the ceiling. Picture sequences can run to six or seven, because they stay on screen and do not have to be held in mind.
One idea per sentence. Compound sentences reliably fail.
Concrete object names work; category words do not.
Idioms, sarcasm and rhetorical questions are taken literally.
Needs to be told when something is finished.
Sustained background noise is the single largest disruptor.
Prefers muted colour and little on-screen movement.
Uses ear defenders on the floor.

worksWell: Pictogram sequences for any physical task
Being told the number of steps before they start
Repetition of the same wording, unchanged
doesNotWork: Spoken-only instruction in a noisy area
Rephrasing the same step differently to be helpful
Being asked to summarise back under time pressure

earlySigns: Repeated adjusting of gloves or sleeves
Moves to the edge of the room
helps: Lower light and stop screen movement
Familiar instrumental audio at low volume
Silence is fine. Do not fill it.
avoid: Asking what is wrong while it is happening
regulation.calmAudioWhy: Stimulus tolerance is low, so a single sustained tone with no melody and no rhythm. Anything with a beat adds load rather than removing it.

companion.why: Long-standing interest. Reduced refusal of new instructions in the first two weeks.

report.review: Six months, or sooner at Alberto's request.

report.name: Dana Ferreira
report.author: Dr Lina Moreau
report.summary: Dana is an autistic adult in the same team as Alberto, with a markedly different profile. She processes spoken language well and prefers it to written material, which she finds effortful to scan. She follows narrative structure easily and remembers instructions better when framed as a sequence with a beginning and an end. Written lists and dense screens are the main barrier.

notes: Spoken instruction lands well. Written lists are read slowly and re-read.
Responds strongly to sequence framing — first, then, last.
Asks clarifying questions readily. Treat as engagement, not confusion.
Prefers to be told the purpose before the steps.
Tolerates ordinary office noise and movement.
Bright flickering light is uncomfortable over long periods.
No difficulty with colour or animation.

worksWell: Spoken instruction with a clear sequence
Framing a task as a short journey
doesNotWork: Written checklists with more than a few items
Dense screens with several things competing
Being handed a document and left to it

earlySigns: Repeats the same question in different words
Stands up and moves without a destination
helps: Speak slowly and stay in the room
Name what is happening next, out loud
Music with a steady predictable structure
Give her something with a clear end point
avoid: Leaving her alone to settle — it escalates
Handing her something written in that moment
regulation.calmAudioWhy: Stimulus tolerance is normal and she settles on structure, so a slow piece with a clear repeating phrase gives her something to follow.

companion.why: Chosen by Dana. The reporter framing suits how she likes tasks explained.

report.review: Six months, or sooner at Dana's request.
